                                     PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
                                   SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

    ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY                       §

    765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE
    PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET,
    CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,
    LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH,
    MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN
    SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,
    AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES


                       INITIAL BRIEF OF LAMPASAS J11 LANDOWNERS


          Introduction

          Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation

applied to amend their certificates of convenience and necessity for the Bell County East Switch

To Big Hill Substation 765-KV transmission line project In Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell,

Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green,

And Williamson counties. The Public Utility Commission of Texas has concluded that the

application is adequate and complies with the requirements in PURA 16 § 22.52(a). 1

          PUC Staff Route 487 Does Not Adequately Reflect Community Values


          The term “community values” is not defined in PURA or the Commission’s rules.

However, the Commission has previously adopted a finding of fact that indicates “community


1
    Poole Direct Testimony Pg.18
                                                1
 values” to be viewed as a “shared appreciation of an area or other natural or human resource by

members of a national, regional, or local community”. 2 Intervention itself is evidence of

community values. The study area included many landowners and communities; not all chose to

participate in this proceeding. Participation in a certificate of convenience and necessity

(“CCN”) requires significant amounts of time, effort and resources. The responses to the official

consultation letters sent to county and city leadership are equivalent to public comment as the

leaders represent constituents in their area and the commonly held values of that community.

        Lampasas County Commissioners and the City Council of Lampasas, as well as the

Lampasas County Water Control and Water Conservation District No. 1, sent letters and passed

resolutions expressing the desire to not have the proposed transmission line in their county or

city. 3 The intervenors along Link J11 and adjacent links on Route 487 in Lampasas County

constitute a community.


        The Intervenors testified that this intrusion would destroy the rural character and

economic value of their ranchland, retirement homes, family heritage, and displace abundant

central-Texas wildlife that currently thrives on the land, and place a large portion of their

property already situated within a regulated floodplain protected by flood-control dam that is

over 70 years old at even greater risk of structural demise, a concern expressly shared by the

county judge, City of Lampasas, and local water district. Additionally, any construction would




2 Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to Amend its Certificate of Convenience and

Necessity (CCN) for a 138 kV Transmission Line Kerr County, Docket No. 33844, Final Order at 15, Finding of
Fact 65 (Mar. 4, 2008).
3 PUC Interchange 433, PUC Interchange 1187, PUC Interchange 27

                                                     2
 disturb Indian burial grounds, an existing navigable water way, federal wetlands, and further

endanger existing endangered species. 4


        The proposed construction of segment J11 would impose profound and lasting

environmental harm on their properties, with multiple housing units within extreme proximity to

the proposed powerlines. Additionally, the segment’s alignment would slice through a very

ecologically sensitive portion of property crossing pristine live-creek frontage on the East Fork

of Sulphur Creek. 5


        The proposed route as previously mentioned is in extreme proximity to the regulated

floodplain protected by an adjoining flood-control dam (Soil Conservation Service Site 6) which

is immediately on the same property. The dam is over 70 years old and was originally

constructed with a 50-year life span. Assuming the lines proposed route were to continue with

the J11 segment, further destabilization of the dam structure itself and similar infrastructure in

the vicinity could create a catastrophic flood risk that could not only endanger but take the lives

of any unfortunate people downstream. 6


        The properties are surrounded by other family-owned ranchland. Much of the acreage and

the area surrounding it is primarily used for cattle pasture, hay cultivation, and wildlife habitat

supporting abundant native species including white-tailed deer, wild turkey, bobwhite quail,




4 Lampasas J11 Landowners Exhibit 3, Direct Testimony of Antal Pataky at 4. Lampasas J11 Landowners

Exhibit 1, Direct Testimony of Todd Lively at 4. Lampasas J11 Landowners Exhibit 2, Direct Testimony of
Stephen Ellison at 4.

        5
            Lively and Ellison Directs at 4.
        6
            Id at 4-5 and PUC Interchange 27.

                                                     3
 numerous songbirds, raptors, and aquatic life dependent on the East Fork of Sulphur Creek flowing

through some of the properties. Some of the properties also include a regulated floodplain

protected by an adjoining Soil Conservation Service Site 6 flood-control dam. 7


             The properties support a mosaic of Central Texas vegetation types, including upland

savannah dominated by iconic plateau live oaks (Quercus fusiformis), post oaks, cedar elms

(Ulmus crassifolia), and scattered Ashe juniper, interspersed with mid- and tall-grass prairie

species such as little bluestem, side oats grama, Texas wintergrass, switchgrass, and Indiangrass

that sustain the abundant wildlife. Along the pristine live-creek frontage and regulated

floodplain, riparian corridors feature bottomland hardwoods including sugarberry, hackberry,

pecan, roughleaf dogwood, and possible bald cypress, with understory layers of saw greenbriar,

poison ivy, knotweed, Emory’s caric sedge, and wetland-tolerant forbs and grasses that stabilize

banks, filter water, and buffer flooding from the adjoining flood-control dam. These ecologically

sensitive plant assemblages nurtured through decades of labor and mortgage payments by the

owners provide critical habitat, erosion control, and biodiversity. J11’s towers, access roads,

and clearing activities within a few hundred feet of homes would fragment this intact vegetative

mosaic, introduce invasive species, accelerate erosion and sedimentation into the creek, and

compromise the very floodplain vegetation that protects regional hydrology. 8


             The Lively and Ellison properties have been actively managed alongside the Texas Parks

and Wildlife Department, with a state game biologist to increase the health and welfare of the

wildlife. It is part of an existing game management association. They also work with the Natural



             7 Id at 6.
8 Id at 7.

                                                    4
 Resources Conservation Service, County Agriculture Extension Agent and have utilized

selective brush management that preserves plateau live oaks, cedar elms, and other canopy

species while controlling invasive Ashe juniper only where necessary and limited grazing that

avoids over-utilization of native mid- and tall-grass prairie (little bluestem, sideoats grama,

indiangrass, switchgrass), and complete protection of the pristine live-creek riparian corridor and

regulated floodplain. They have maintained intact travel corridors, nesting cover, and foraging

areas for abundant native wildlife including white-tailed deer, wild turkey, bobwhite quail,

songbirds, raptors, and aquatic species and harvested game animals in accordance with the

recommendations of the wildlife biologists. Riparian buffers have been left virtually undisturbed

to stabilize banks, filter runoff, and support bottomland hardwoods and understory vegetation,

thereby complementing the adjoining flood-control dam and reducing sedimentation risks.

Supplemental water features from the perennial creek, combined with natural food sources from

diverse forbs, grasses, and mast-producing trees, have sustained this self-sustaining ecosystem

without heavy reliance on artificial feeding or intensive intervention. The routing of segment J11

within a few hundred feet of their home would fragment these carefully preserved habitats,

introduce construction disturbance and access roads through sensitive areas, and permanently

degrade the very wildlife values they have invested decades of labor to protect, and totally

devastate their retirement home and well-being. 9




9
    Pataky at 5-6. Id at 7-8.



                                                  5
 There are Many Alternatives, including Route 894, Which Avoid the Devastating

Environmental Impact of a New Colorado River Crossing in A Pristine Area on Link J11.


       The Applicants recommend and support Route 894 as the best meets route in comparison

with other alternatives, as it was the most compliant with Commission rules and policies

regarding routing.


       “A     My selection of Route 894, which consists of links AO-A1-A2-B1-B21-C4-

                      D12-C5-E52-F1-F31-F32-F20-F23-G72-G73-G82-G13-G51-G52-H1-

H41-                          H42-J21-J22-J23-J27-J4-K11-K7 -J16-K13-K51-K52-M11-M12-

N3-P2-R1-                            T1-T2-Z2, is based on the factors in PURA§

37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D), 16 TAC

              § 25.101 (including the Commission's policy of prudent avoidance), the

       Commission's CCN

              application form, the information provided to me by Ms. Cooley regarding cost

              Estimates and engineering constraints, the information included in the

              Environmental Assessment and Routing Study, my personal reconnaissance of the

              study area, and information gathered via other Halff,        Kimley-Horn, Oncor,

                      and LCRA TSC employees' reconnaissance of the study area. As

              presented in the Application, I also recommend that the Commission consider the

              121 additional alternative    routes as potential alternatives to Route 894. All




                                               6
 122 routes included in the           Application comply with the routing requirements

of PURA            § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and 16 TAC§ 25.101.” 10

Petty further testifies:


“PLEASE EXPLAIN THE BASIS FOR YOUR SELECTION OF ROUTE 894.


A. Kimley-Horn and Halff provided me with information on 1,246

      alternative routes in the Environmental Assessment and Routing Study.

      After analyzing those 1,246 alternative routes, I recommended filing 122

      of those routes with the Application for the Commission's consideration.

      In addition to geographic differences, the more significant differences

      between the 122 filed alternative routes are route lengths and costs.

      Route lengths for the filed alternative routes range from approximately

      214.0 miles to 244.4 miles. The estimated project costs for the filed

      alternative routes, excluding station costs, range from approximately

      $1,636,232,000 to $1,857,768,000. Ms. Cooley discusses the breakdown

      of total estimated project costs, including transmission line costs and

      station costs, in her direct testimony. Given the balance of the factors, I

      selected Route 894 as the route that best meets the requirements of

      PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and 16 TAC § 25.101.            Specifically, this




10
     Direct Testimony of Casey Petty at 12.


                                         7
                        route, as compared to the other filed alternative routes included in the

                       Application:


                   •        is approximately 223.7 miles in length, which is 9.7 miles longer than the

                   shortest filed route and approximately 20.7 miles shorter than the longest filed

                   route;


                   •        has an estimated transmission line cost of $1,680,919,000, which is

                   approximately 2.73% more than the least costly filed route and 18 9.52% less

                   than the most costly filed route; and


                   •        has 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of its centerline, which is five

                   more than the filed routes with the fewest habitable structures within 500 feet of

                   their centerlines and 99 less than the filed routes with the most habitable

                   structures within 500 feet of their centerlines.


                   My routing memorandum, Exhibit CDP-6, lays out additional factors I considered

                   in selecting Route 894. In addition, Route 894, like the other filed routes, was

                   judged to be feasible from an engineering perspective based on currently known

                            conditions, without the benefit of on-the-ground and subsurface surveys,

                   as further discussed in the direct testimony of Ms. Cooley. “ 11


         On cross-examination by Lampasas J11 Landowners, Oncor witness Marusak also

testified that the Applicants carefully studied all potential crossing points of the Colorado and




11 Id. at 12-14.

                                                      8
 that Link J22, on route 894 was the place which best meets all Commission criteria for such a

crossing.


        The selection of Route 487 as the preferred route by PUC Staff was not conducted

using any weighting criteria or other data analysis. Route 487 selected by PUC Staff only

has the appearance of standing out when compared to the extremes of the other routes in

the Environmental Assessment.

        Additionally, on cross – examination PUC witness Poole confirmed that link J11 crosses

within 100 feet of the entrance to Colorado Bend State Park. 12 He also confirmed that this was a

“problem “with his original recommendation. He additionally admitted that there are good

reasons to cross where there is already an existing transmission line crossing.


        Several other intervenor witnesses, including Dr. Andrew Sansom for Wullf Bluff Creek

Ranch also supported using different links from J11 to cross the Colorado. Sansom conducts a

careful analysis of the potential crossing points. “Based on my review of materials in the

Application, the central crossing locations involving Links U2 and Jll are among those most

proximate to Colorado Bend State Park and other notable natural features along the river

corridor. The proximity of those crossings to highly valued recreational and natural areas

warrants careful consideration of potential visual, environmental, and long-term corridor

impacts.” He ultimately recommends Link U3. 13


        “Link U3 crosses the Colorado River in a location that parallels existing electric

transmission infrastructure, whereas every other link that crosses the Colorado River would



12 See also Poole Direct Testimony at 40.
13 Direct Testimony of Andrew H. Sansom at 8-13.

                                                   9
 create a new crossing corridor. By utilizing Link U3, the proposed transmission line would

consolidate infrastructure within an existing corridor rather than introducing a whole new

crossing location.” 14


        “If the Commission finds that the Applicants have presented a route or routes that meet

the statutory and regulatory standards, the Commission should avoid approving a crossing of

the Colorado River at a previously undisturbed area.” 15


        Cherokee Creek witness Reinecke notes that J11 is one of the links which crosses the

Colorado at a TPWD designated Ecologically Significant Stream Segment.


        “Q: WHY IS THE COLORADO RIVER CROSSING IMPORTANT TO YOUR

ANALYSIS?


        A: The Colorado River serves as major a hydrologic and biological corridor through the

broader region. Portions of the river provide USFWS-designated critical habitat for species listed

and proposed under the ESA and are recognized by TPWD as ESSS. Thus, the Colorado River

crossing should not be evaluated merely as one additional stream crossing in a numerical count.

A crossing of the Colorado River may affect not only the river channel itself, but also the

associated riparian corridor, adjacent woodland, wildlife movement, scenic quality, and

recreational experience in the surrounding area. Given the overall project alignment, all route

alternatives must cross the feature at some point. So, given that it cannot be avoided, I evaluated




14 Direct Testimony of Dr. Joshua Rhodes on behalf of Solana Ranch, et.al. at 13. emph. supp.
15 Direct Testimony of Barry T. Smitherman on behalf of Save the Lampasas et.al at 21. emph. supp.

                                                      10
 the location and context of the proposed link crossings to see if there were opportunities to

minimize potential impact.


        Q: WHERE IS THE PORTION OF THE COLORADO RIVER WITHIN THE STUDY

AREA DESIGNATED AS AN ESSS?


        A: The ESSS-designated segment extends from where the Colorado River enters the

northern edge of the Study Area downstream to its confluence with Yancey Creek, just north of

the 22 Lampasas/Burnet County line. As reflected in Table RLSR-7, Links U3, U2, and Jll cross

the designated ESSS portion of the Colorado River. These are the three northernmost proposed

crossings of the river within the Study Area.


        Q: DID YOU NOTICE ANY ADDITIONAL DIFFERENCES AMONG THE

PROPOSED COLORADO RIVER CROSSINGS?


        A: Yes. I observed two notable distinctions. First, the Colorado River crossings

associated with Links Jll, J22, and J26 are located in relatively close proximity to Colorado Bend

State Park and/or Post Oak Ridge State Park. That proximity may compound the potential

impacts of a transmission line crossing because it combines major river crossing impacts with

potential visual, scenic, and recreational effects on nearby public park resources.” She then

recommends Link J31. 16


        Hodge and Schwertner’s witness Brian Andrews also supports avoidance of the Link J11

area.




16 Direct Testimony of Rae Lynn Schneider Reinecke on behalf of Segment K13/K51 Landowners at 42-43.

                                                  11
        “Q ARE THERE UNIQUE CIRCUMSTANCES IN THIS PROCEEDING?


        A. Yes. All 122 filed alternative routes must cross the Colorado River to connect the Bell

County East Switch with the Big Hill Substation in Schleicher County. Colorado Bend State

Park (approximately 5,300 acres) and Post Oak Ridge State Park (approximately 7 3,170 acres)

lie along the Colorado River in the central portion of the study area, occupying approximately

8,500 acres collectively. Post Oak Ridge State Park was one of the first three parks acquired

using the voter-approved $1 billion Centennial Parks Conservation Fund, underscoring the public

significance of this resource. Because the location of each Colorado River crossing relative to

these two state parks varies across the filed routes, the visual impact analysis presented in

Section 7.7 of the Environmental Assessment is an important consideration in this proceeding.

The Application includes multiple routes that avoid foreground visual impacts on these state

parks with otherwise comparable routing-factor performance and only modest estimated cost

differences.


       Q WHICH LINKS PASS WITHIN THE FOREGROUND VISUAL ZONE OF THE

STATE PARKS, AND WHICH ROUTES DO NOT USE THOSE LINKS?


       A. Two links pass within the half-mile foreground visual zone of one or both of the state

parks in the study area: Link Jll and Link J26. Across the 122 filed routes, ROW within the

foreground visual zone of state parks and recreational areas ranges from 0.00 miles to 8.68 miles.

Per Section 7.7.5 of the Environmental Assessment, Link Jll is approximately 100 feet from the

northern boundary of Colorado Bend State Park and spans Colorado Park Road, the park's

primary entrance road. The park's main entrance and fee booth, approximately 1.5 miles of the

Tie Slide Trail, the River Overlook, and approximately one mile of the Gorman Falls Trail are
                                                 12
 within the half-mile foreground visual zone of Link J11. Twenty-five of the 122 filed routes use

Link J11.” Andrews ultimately recommended Route 894. 17


                                                 Conclusion


        The construction of a route that includes segment J11 would pass directly through the

middle of Intervenor properties within a few hundred feet of family homes, devastating the most

valuable road-frontage acreage, the field used for farming, grazing, hunting, etc. and the pristine

live-creek frontage that forms the heart of our ranch. This would permanently fragment and

destroy diverse native plant communities including plateau live oaks, cedar elms, native prairie

grasses, and sensitive riparian vegetation they have managed for generations; displace abundant

Central Texas wildlife and create extreme stress on all domestic animals and all other wildlife.


        The proposed route 487 would cross sensitive creek and floodplain areas near an existing

flood-control dam, raising the very risks to regional hydrology and downstream water resources

that have already prompted documented concern from the local water district; any compromise

to that infrastructure could increase flooding threats to neighboring properties, roads, and

agricultural lands throughout the area. Furthermore, by fragmenting intact wildlife corridors and

native habitats that support abundant Central Texas game and songbird populations, the line

would degrade the rural character and recreational value of our entire community. Approval of

this route would also threaten the viability of family farms and ranches that define their shared

way of life, and introduce industrial-scale visual, noise, and safety intrusions into a landscape

long prized for its peace and natural beauty. We believe the Commission must weigh these




17 Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews on behalf of Hodge and Schwertner parties at 13-14.

                                                    13
 cumulative community harms against any claimed need for the line to be here, as the permanent

loss of rural heritage, ecological services, and quality of life for so many families far outweighs

any localized benefit.


        The Commission should reject any route that includes Link J11, as it would unnecessarily

impact a single, contiguous, and interconnected landscape and the surrounding ranchlands.

Together, these areas form one of the most intact, unspoiled, and carefully preserved landscapes

in Central Texas.


        The effects of Link J11 would extend well beyond any single property. It would fragment

an otherwise cohesive ecological corridor, degrade a landscape of recognized historical and

cultural significance, needlessly create a new and unsightly crossing of the Colorado River and

adversely affect the broader community that depends on these resources for identity, recreation,

and economic activity. These impacts would not be isolated or temporary, but structural and

enduring.


        Instead, the Commission should select a route that minimizes environmental impact,

avoids fragmentation of intact ranchland and wildlife habitat, and preserves the integrity of this

landscape, including unnecessary new and intrusive crossings of the Colorado River. That

includes protecting not only individual features, but the continuity, context, and views that give

this area its significance.


        WHEREFORE, PREMISES CONSIDEDRED, Lampasas J11 Landowners respectfully

request that Route 487, including Link J11, no longer be considered as any part of the route to be

considered for any transmission line, as it will have such a devastating and detrimental impact on


                                                 14
 its property, as well as the crossing of an untouched pristine area of the Colorado Rivere. We

further recommend Route 894, or a similar alternative avoiding Link J11, to be selected and for

such further and other relief as may be granted.


                                              Respectively submitted,

                                                 Conclusion


        The construction of a route that includes segment Jl 1 would pass directly through the

middle of Intervenor properties within a few hundred feet of family homes, devastating the most

valuable road-frontage acreage, the field used for farming, grazing, hunting, etc. and the pristine

live-creek frontage that forms the heart of our ranch. This would permanently fragment and

destroy diverse native plant communities including plateau live oaks, cedar elms, native prairie

grasses, and sensitive riparian vegetation they have managed for generations; displace abundant

Central Texas wildlife and create extreme stress on all domestic animals and all other wildlife.


        The proposed route 487 would cross sensitive creek and floodplain areas near an existing

flood-control dam, raising the very risks to regional hydrology and downstream water resources

that have already prompted documented concern from the local water district; any compromise

to that infrastructure could increase flooding threats to neighboring properties, roads, and

agricultural lands throughout the area. Furthermore, by fragmenting intact wildlife corridors and

native habitats that support abundant Central Texas game and songbird populations, the line

would degrade the rural character and recreational value of our entire community. Approval of

this route would also threaten the viability of family farms and ranches that define their shared

way of life, and introduce industrial-scale visual, noise, and safety intrusions into a landscape

long prized for its peace and natural beauty. We believe the Commission must weigh these

 cumulative community harms against any claimed need for the line to be here, as the permanent

loss of rural heritage, ecological services, and quality of life for so many families far outweighs

        The Commission should reject any route that includes Link Jl 1, as it would unnecessarily

impact a single, contiguous, and interconnected landscape and the surrounding ranchlands.

Together, these areas form one of the most intact, unspoiled, and carefully preserved landscapes

in Central Texas.


        The effects of Link Jl l would extend well beyond any single property. It would fragment

an otherwise cohesive ecological corridor, degrade a landscape of recognized historical and

cultural significance, needlessly create a new and unsightly crossing of the Colorado River and

adversely affect the broader community that depends on these resources for identity, recreation,

and economic activity. These impacts would not be isolated or temporary, but structural and

enduring.


        Instead, the Commission should select a route that minimizes environmental impact,

avoids fragmentation of intact ranchland and wildlife habitat, and preserves the integrity of this

landscape, including unnecessary new and intrusive crossings ofthe Colorado River. That

includes protecting not only individual features, but the continuity, context, and views that give

this area its significance.
